children.value: Lifecycle data: updates, signing, and trust
Offing's findings come from lifecycle rules (

). The rules that ship inside each release are always available. Between releases you can fetch newer rules, which are signed so that Offing can tell they came from the project's release workflow. This page explains how that works, what is checked, and what Offing promises.
read local files only. The only command that connects to anything is
, and it runs only when you run it. A test fails if any other code path opens a socket, resolves a name, or calls
Downloaded data is verified before it is used, every time it is loaded.
If it cannot be verified, Offing uses the data shipped with the installed release and says so in the result. It never loads data it could not verify.
You can see how fresh the evidence is.
Every scan and check says which data it used and how old it is, and warns when that is more than 30 days.
You can fix the data version
Updating asks a public release list and downloads public files. Nothing about you or your repository is sent.

offing data status                       # which data is in use, where it came from, how old it is (--json for tools)
offing data update                       # fetch and verify the newest signed bundle
offing data update --data-version 2026.10.01   # fetch exactly that bundle, without making it active
offing scan . --data-version 2026.10.01  # use exactly that bundle (every command takes this)
OFFING_DATA_VERSION=bundled offing scan .   # use only the data shipped with this release
(the version you asked for). Its age is counted from when a downloaded bundle was built, or from the newest review date among the rules for bundled data.

releases, picks the newest one that has a bundle and a signature, downloads both (https only, with size limits and timeouts), verifies them completely, and only then stores them in your cache and makes them active. If anything is wrong the previous data stays active and nothing is written. Running it again when nothing changed says so.

It refuses a bundle that is older than the active one (a replayed old bundle would roll your rules back), a bundle the installed release already beats, and anything that fails verification. Three bundles are kept.

Offing accepts a bundle only if
The signature verifies against the exact bytes downloaded (certificate chain, validity period, transparency-log inclusion).
The signer is the project's release workflow: issuer
A valid signature from any other workflow, repository, or branch is refused.

The certificates and log keys come from the Sigstore public-good trusted root, which ships in the

) so that verification needs no network. That is also why you should keep Offing reasonably current: if Sigstore rotates its keys and the root in your installed release is too old, signatures made after the rotation stop verifying. Offing then falls back to its bundled data and tells you; it does not skip the check.

What this does not protect against
A compromise of the repository's release workflow or of a maintainer with permission to push a
tag: the workflow would sign whatever it was given. Rule changes are reviewed before they reach
, and the signature proves where a bundle came from, not that its contents are correct.
A compromised Offing package: the trusted root and the signer identity are part of the release you installed.
Wrong evidence. Signing says who published a rule, not that the claim is true; each rule cites its sources and review date for that reason.
, a tamper-evident log of all data releases so far, with its own keyless signature (
). Each line is one release: version,

, the SHA-256 of the bundle file, the build time, the hash of the previous line, and its own hash. Because every entry commits to the one before it, changing, removing, or reordering a past release changes every later hash.

The release workflow downloads the previous release's log, refuses one that does not verify, appends the new bundle, and requires the result to extend the old log before signing it. The signatures of the bundle and of the log are recorded in the public Sigstore transparency log (Rekor), so a quiet rewrite would need the log's hashes and Rekor's entries to change together.
Check a log, and optionally that it extends an older copy you kept:

gh release download data-vYYYY.MM.DD --repo velella-sh/ebb --pattern 'release-log.jsonl*'
node dist/tools/data-release-log.js check release-log.jsonl --previous older-release-log.jsonl   # in a checkout of Ebb
The first release made after this was added starts the log; earlier releases are not listed.
